screens.title: Windows Privilege Model
screens.narratorSegment: Just like in Linux, gaining initial access to a Windows system often leaves you with the privileges of a standard user. However, the Windows privilege model operates quite differently from Linux. Instead of simple user IDs and group IDs, Windows relies on Security Identifiers, or SIDs, which are unique values assigned to users, groups, and other security principals. These SIDs are then used in Access Control Lists, or ACLs, which define permissions on objects like files, folders, and registry keys. The most powerful account on a Windows machine is the SYSTEM account. This account has extensive control over the operating system and its resources, far beyond what a typical Administrator account possesses. Understanding these core components – SIDs, ACLs, and the SYSTEM account – is fundamental to identifying and exploiting privilege escalation vulnerabilities. For example, if a service runs as SYSTEM but has weak ACLs on its executable, a low-privileged user might be able to replace that executable, effectively running their own code with SYSTEM privileges. This distinction is crucial for effective Windows penetration testing. Windows Privilege Model means windows uses sids and acls, with system being the highest privilege, unlike linux's uid/gid model.. In practical terms, understanding sids, acls, and the system account. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5›Chapter 3›Windows Privilege Model
Core Concept

Windows Privilege Model

Understanding SIDs, ACLs, and the SYSTEM Account

Key Components

  • •
    Security Identifiers (SIDs): Unique values identifying users, groups, and security principals.
  • •
    Access Control Lists (ACLs): Define permissions on objects (files, registry keys) based on SIDs.
  • •
    SYSTEM Account: The most powerful local account, with extensive control over the OS.

Example: Weak ACLs

Imagine a service running as SYSTEM, but its executable file has weak ACLs allowing a standard user to modify it. An attacker could replace the legitimate executable with a malicious one, gaining SYSTEM privileges when the service restarts.

Pro Tip

Always check file and directory permissions for services running with high privileges.

screens.title: Unquoted Service Paths
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most common and often overlooked privilege escalation vectors on Windows is the unquoted service path vulnerability. This occurs when a service executable's path contains spaces but is not enclosed in quotation marks. Windows, in its attempt to resolve the path, may misinterpret it. Let's consider an example: if a service path is C. backslash Program Files backslash My Application backslash service. exe and it's unquoted, Windows will try to execute C. backslash Program. exe first. If that fails, it then tries C. backslash Program Files backslash My. exe, and only then C. backslash Program Files backslash My Application backslash service. exe. The critical vulnerability here is that if an attacker can place a malicious executable named Program. exe in C. backslash Program Files backslash, and that service runs with elevated privileges like SYSTEM, the malicious executable will be executed instead of the legitimate one. This is a classic example of a path resolution vulnerability. It's a subtle but powerful flaw that can be exploited to gain high privileges without needing complex kernel exploits. Understanding this mechanism is key to both exploiting and defending against this common attack.

keyIdea.text: Unquoted service paths allow Windows to execute malicious binaries placed in intermediate directories.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 3›Vulnerability Spotlight
Vulnerability Spotlight

Unquoted Service Paths

How Windows misinterprets service executable paths

The Core Problem

  • •
    Service path contains spaces but no quotation marks.
  • •
    Windows attempts to execute each segment of the path.
  • •
    An attacker can place a malicious executable in an earlier segment.

Vulnerable Path Example

C:\Program Files\My Application\service.exe

If unquoted, Windows will first try to execute `C:\Program.exe`, then `C:\Program Files\My.exe`, before finally reaching the intended `service.exe`.

Key Takeaway

This vulnerability allows for arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the vulnerable service.

Unquoted Path Resolution

Original Path

`C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe`

Attempt 1

`C:\Program.exe`

Attempt 2

`C:\Program Files\My.exe`

Attempt 3 (Legitimate)

`C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe`

screens.title: Finding Unquoted Service Paths with `wmic`
screens.narratorSegment: Now that you understand the concept of unquoted service paths, let's look at how to discover them on a compromised Windows machine. The wmic command is an incredibly useful built-in tool for this purpose. You can use it to query service configurations and filter for specific characteristics. The command we use is wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode pipe findstr slash i "auto" pipe findstr slash i slash v "c. backslash windows backslash backslash ". Let's break this down: first, we're getting the name, display name, path name, and start mode for all services. Then, we're filtering for services that are set to 'auto' start, meaning they'll run automatically when the system boots. Finally, and crucially, we're excluding paths that start with c. backslash windows backslash. This is because services located in the Windows directory are typically legitimate and properly quoted. What you're looking for in the output are Path Name values that contain spaces but are not enclosed in quotation marks. If you find one, you've identified a potential target for privilege escalation. This command is a powerful and efficient way to quickly scan for this common vulnerability, providing actionable intelligence for your next steps.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 3›Discovery Technique
Discovery Technique

Finding Unquoted Service Paths with `wmic`

Identifying vulnerable services on a target system

The `wmic` Command Explained

  • •
    `wmic service get ...`: Queries service properties.
  • •
    `findstr /i "auto"`: Filters for auto-start services.
  • •
    `findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\"`: Excludes legitimate Windows paths.

Command to Execute

wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\"
Key Takeaway

Look for `PathName` values with spaces and no quotes outside of `C:\Windows` directories.

Interpreting `wmic` Output

Legitimate (Quoted)

`"C:\Program Files\App\service.exe"`

Vulnerable (Unquoted)

`C:\Program Files\Vulnerable App\service.exe`

Actionable Insight

Place malicious `Program.exe` in `C:\Program Files\`

screens.narratorSegment: Beyond unquoted service paths, another significant area for privilege escalation involves service misconfigurations, specifically weak permissions on service executables or their configuration. This type of misconfiguration is surprisingly common, especially in older systems or custom applications where security best practices weren't strictly followed during installation. It's a direct path to high privileges, making it a prime target for attackers. Understanding how to identify and exploit these weak permissions is a fundamental skill in Windows privilege escalation. Module 5›Chapter 3›Service Vulnerabilities
Service Vulnerabilities

Service Misconfigurations: Weak ACLs

Exploiting weak permissions on service executables

The Misconfiguration

  • •
    Service runs with high privileges (e.g., SYSTEM).
  • •
    Executable file or its directory has weak ACLs.
  • •
    Low-privileged user can modify or replace the executable.

Exploitation Scenario

An attacker replaces a legitimate service executable with a malicious reverse shell. When the service restarts, the reverse shell executes with SYSTEM privileges, granting the attacker full control.

Key Takeaway

Always check permissions on service binaries and their containing directories, especially for services running as SYSTEM.

Weak ACLs Attack Flow

Identify High-Privilege Service

e.g., runs as SYSTEM

Check ACLs on Executable/Directory

Look for write permissions for low-privileged users

Replace Executable with Payload

Inject malicious code

Restart Service

Execute payload with SYSTEM privileges

screens.title: Querying Service Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: To effectively exploit service misconfigurations, you first need to identify them. This involves querying a service's configuration and checking its file permissions. The sc qc command is your go-to for querying a service's configuration. By running sc qc, you can retrieve details like the service's binary path and the account it runs under. Module 5›Chapter 3›Discovery Technique
Discovery Technique

Querying Service Permissions

Using `sc qc` and `icacls` to check service configurations

Tools for Inspection

  • •
    `sc qc `: Queries service configuration (binary path, run account).
  • •
    `icacls `: Displays and modifies file/directory ACLs.
  • •

Example: Checking Permissions

# Query service config
sc qc "Vulnerable Service"

# Check permissions on its binary
icacls "C:\Program Files\Vulnerable App\service.exe"
Key Takeaway

Look for 'Write' or 'Modify' permissions for 'Everyone' or 'Authenticated Users' on high-privilege service binaries.

List Services

Identify services of interest

Query Service Config (`sc qc`)

Get binary path and run account

Check File/Directory ACLs (`icacls`)

Determine write permissions

Exploit if Weak ACLs Found

Replace binary and restart service

screens.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Registry Setting
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond services, specific registry settings can also open doors for privilege escalation. The 'AlwaysInstallElevated' registry setting is a classic example of such a vulnerability. If both the HKCU backslash SOFTWARE backslash Policies backslash Microsoft backslash Windows backslash Installer and HKLM backslash SOFTWARE backslash Policies backslash Microsoft backslash Windows backslash Installer keys have the Always Install Elevated value set to 1, it signifies a critical misconfiguration. When this setting is enabled, it means that any user, regardless of their current privilege level, can install Windows Installer, or MSI, packages with SYSTEM privileges. This is a significant security flaw because it bypasses the normal User Account Control, or UAC, mechanisms. An attacker can leverage this by creating a malicious MSI package, perhaps using a tool like msfvenom, that executes a reverse shell or adds a new administrative user. Then, by simply installing this malicious package, the attacker can gain SYSTEM access. This vulnerability highlights how seemingly innocuous system configurations can have profound security implications, offering a direct path to the highest privileges on a Windows system. It's a powerful technique to be aware of.

Module 5›Chapter 3›Registry Vulnerability
Registry Vulnerability

AlwaysInstallElevated Registry Setting

Allowing non-admin users to install with SYSTEM privileges

The Vulnerability

  • •
    `AlwaysInstallElevated` set to `1` in both HKCU and HKLM.
  • •
    Bypasses User Account Control (UAC).
  • •
    Allows any user to install MSI packages with SYSTEM privileges.

Exploitation Example

An attacker creates a malicious MSI package (e.g., with `msfvenom`) that executes a reverse shell. By installing this package, the attacker gains a SYSTEM shell.

Key Takeaway

This setting is a direct path to SYSTEM privileges and should always be disabled in secure environments.

AlwaysInstallElevated Flow

Check Registry Keys

HKCU & HKLM `AlwaysInstallElevated` = 1

Create Malicious MSI

e.g., `msfvenom` reverse shell

Install MSI as Low-Privilege User

Installation runs with SYSTEM

Gain SYSTEM Access

Full control over the system

screens.title: Automating Discovery with PowerShell Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Manually checking for all these privilege escalation vectors can be time-consuming and prone to error. This is where PowerShell scripts become incredibly powerful for automating the discovery process. Tools like Power Up. ps1, which is part of the PowerSploit framework, are specifically designed to enumerate a wide range of common Windows privilege escalation vulnerabilities. This includes everything we've discussed, such as unquoted service paths, weak service executable permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated checks, and even other opportunities like DLL hijacking. To use it, you typically load Power Up. ps1 into memory on the target system, for example, by using powershell -ep bypass -file Power Up. ps1, and then execute functions like Invoke-All Checks. The script provides detailed, color-coded output, making it much easier to identify actionable vulnerabilities at a glance. However, it's important to remember that Windows Defender and other Endpoint Detection and Response, or EDR, solutions might detect Power Up. ps1 due to its known malicious use. Therefore, in real-world engagements, stealthy execution methods or obfuscation might be necessary to avoid detection. This automation significantly boosts your efficiency in finding escalation paths.
